opus-5.5.text:
To me, taste in infrastructure is mostly about knowing what *not* to build. There are always a hundred things you could optimize, a hundred knobs you could expose, and a hundred features people ask for. Taste is picking the few abstractions that will still make sense a year or two from now, when the models, the hardware, and the workloads have all changed.

A few things come to mind when I think about it.

First, finding the right abstraction boundary. A good system has a core that is small and principled, and everything else can be layered on top. If you get that core right, new optimizations slot in naturally. If you get it wrong, every new model architecture or hardware generation becomes a painful rewrite. A lot of taste is sensing early which concepts are fundamental, like how you manage memory, how you schedule requests, or how you represent the computation, and which ones are incidental to today's models.

Second, being driven by real workloads and not by benchmarks alone. It's easy to make a number look good on a microbenchmark. But taste means asking: what are people actually going to run? Long contexts, multi-turn agents, structured outputs, lots of shared prefixes? When you look at real usage patterns, you often discover the bottleneck is somewhere nobody was looking, and the most impactful design is the one that matches how people really use the system.

Third, simplicity for the user, even when the inside is complicated. The best infrastructure feels boring to use. Developers shouldn't have to understand every scheduling detail to get good performance. So you take on the complexity internally and keep the interface clean, which is harder than it sounds, because there's always a temptation to push complexity out to the user as configuration.

And finally, I think taste includes timing. Some ideas are right but too early, and some are obvious but nobody has done them well yet. Part of the judgment is recognizing when the ecosystem is ready, when the hardware, the models, and the community needs line up, so that a design choice actually gets adopted instead of just being clever.

So if I had to sum it up, taste is the combination of deep technical understanding and restraint: knowing the system well enough to see what really matters, and being disciplined enough to build only that, and build it well.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes a small, principled core, sound abstraction boundaries, and disciplined internal complexity, communicating that infrastructure taste includes the quality of the design itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because "taste" sounds like such a vague word, and infrastructure is supposed to be the least vague thing in the world. But I do think it's real, and I'll try to describe what it feels like from the inside.

To me, taste in systems design is mostly about knowing what not to build. Anyone who has worked on an inference engine like SGLang, or really any serving system, knows that at every step there are ten features you could add. Every one of them has a user asking for it. Taste is the ability to look at those ten and say, these two belong in the core, these five should be plugins or live outside the system entirely, and these three we should say no to, even if that disappoints someone today. The hardest part of that is that the "no" usually looks wrong in the short term. You only find out it was right six months later, when the codebase is still something people can read.

The second part is choosing the right abstraction boundary. In the LLM serving world, a good example is how you separate scheduling from kernel execution, or how you think about the KV cache as a first-class object rather than something hidden inside a model forward pass. When you pick the boundary well, a lot of things that would have been special cases just fall out naturally. Prefix sharing, speculative decoding, structured output, they all become composable instead of being hacks bolted on. When you pick it badly, every new feature touches every file, and you can feel that pain even if you can't name the mistake. I think taste is partly the accumulated memory of having felt that pain enough times that you can anticipate it.

The third thing, and this one is maybe less glamorous, is caring about what the system feels like to the person using it at 2 a.m. when something is broken. Good infrastructure gives you a clear mental model. When you look at a metric or a log line, you should be able to guess what happened without reading the source. Performance matters a lot, obviously, that's half of why people come to these systems. But I've seen plenty of fast systems that nobody wants to operate, and that's a failure of taste too. Simplicity isn't a nice-to-have, it's what lets you move fast a year from now instead of just this quarter.

And I'd add one more thing. Taste is not the same as being clever. Some of the designs I'm proudest of look almost boring when you explain them. The elegance is that they handle a very broad range of workloads with very few concepts. If you need a whiteboard and twenty minutes to explain why the design is good, it may still be a good design, but it probably isn't a tasteful one.

So if I had to compress it: taste is the ability to say no, to pick boundaries that make future work easy, and to value the operator's experience as much as the benchmark number. You develop it by building things, watching them break, and being honest with yourself about why.

r001.rationale: The response describes taste as choosing sound abstractions, keeping systems simple and readable, and making them operable—not merely optimizing performance or meeting a benchmark.

astra-6.text:
To me, taste in infrastructure design is knowing where to put the complexity. You can’t eliminate all of it, but you can decide whether every application developer has to deal with it or whether the infrastructure can handle it behind a clear interface.

Say you’re designing a distributed system. The interface might look very simple when everything works. But what happens when a request times out? Did the operation fail, or did it succeed and the response get lost? A good design gives people a way to reason about that. Simplicity has to survive failures.

Taste also means knowing what not to build. Engineers can be drawn to a general solution that handles every possible future requirement. I’d rather start with the constraints we actually understand, make the tradeoffs explicit, and leave room to evolve.

So I think of taste as judgment: choosing abstractions that make the common case easy, keep the difficult cases understandable, and remain useful as the system grows.

r001.rationale: The response defines taste through choices about complexity, interfaces, failure handling, and abstractions, showing concern for the system’s design quality beyond simply making it work.

sol-6.1.text:
To me, having taste in infrastructure system design means knowing where complexity belongs—and where it doesn’t need to exist at all. You can build something very sophisticated, but if it’s hard to operate, hard to debug, or hard for another engineer to understand, I wouldn’t necessarily call that good design.

A lot of taste shows up in the tradeoffs. What do you make easy? What constraints do you expose? What do you deliberately leave out? You need to understand the workload and the people using the system well enough to make those choices.

And I think taste includes restraint. You can anticipate how a system might evolve without building every possible future into the first version. A design I like solves the current problem clearly and gives you room to change your mind as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates infrastructure design by its complexity, operability, debuggability, and understandability, showing that taste concerns the system’s design quality beyond merely solving the current problem.
